Starry Maroon Bells

memories below

Maroon After Midnight

The red shows up long before the Bells do. Driving up the Maroon Creek valley, the walls turn from green to rust, then to cliffs banded in rose and cream above the aspens and spruce. That is the Maroon Formation, iron-red sediment washed off an older mountain range and turned to rock, and it is where the Bells get their name. By the time I reached the lake that evening, the peaks had gone a hazy blue-gray, backlit, with old snow still hanging on in late July. The water was dark and nearly still. Maroon Peak and North Maroon Peak, both over fourteen thousand feet, hardly needed my help.

The first time I came, we hiked in with backpacks to the edge of the treeline and slept in hammocks through a freezing night. This time the gear rode in a Jeep. Camp was a rooftop tent, a tarp strung between the aspens and a little camp kitchen, all in a grove beside a creek. Hardly roughing it, but I won't pretend a steaming pot on a camp table doesn't beat a freezing hammock. Nearly eight years on, the Bells looked exactly as I remembered them. Mountains are patient like that. They wait for us to come back older and better equipped.

Near midnight I stepped out to the creek with my camera and pointed it straight up. A valley that famous goes quiet once the sun is gone. There was only the creek, and above the aspens and spruce a faint band of Milky Way, with a warm glow from camp lighting the leaves from below. The long exposures smoothed the creek and stretched a lantern's reflection across the dark water. The sky puts this on every clear night, and I'm glad I stayed up to see it.
